fieldContract.extractionId: Stable identifier for one extraction record. Format X-G####.
fieldContract.recordId: The screening-flow recordId this extraction belongs to. One-to-one.
fieldContract.proposedSourceId: The lowercase kebab-case entity ID Codex should use if this extraction is promoted to a sourceSchema record. Proposed, not authoritative: Codex owns content/sources/.
fieldContract.sourceSchemaFields: Fields shaped to sourceSchema in src/lib/content/schemas.ts, minus the lifecycle fields Codex owns. study{} is deliberately absent: population, sampleSize, durationWeeks, intervention, comparator and outcomes are recorded inside extraction.reportedFacts with their locators, so that no study fact appears anywhere without the exact place it came from. projectSummary is likewise absent because a published summary must be written against an approved claim set, which does not exist yet.
fieldContract.sourceSchemaFields.publication.stage: Uses the four-value enum frozen by the SBLA-009 prerequisite decisions: peer-reviewed, preprint, other-non-peer-reviewed, not-applicable. Book and Bookshelf chapters are other-non-peer-reviewed.
fieldContract.sourceSchemaFields.publication.status: current unless a status check found otherwise. corrected is set where Crossref reports an updated-by erratum.
fieldContract.sourceSchemaFields.funding and .conflict: null means not extracted in this pass rather than absent in the source. Funding and conflict statements were read for the full-text sources and are recorded inside reportedFacts where present; they were not systematically transcribed into these two fields, and that gap is limitation L-6.
fieldContract.extraction.reportedFacts: What the source states, each with a locator and a basis. basis is full-text, abstract-only, metadata, or a machine-translated variant of those. Nothing in this array is interpretation.
fieldContract.extraction.authorsInterpretation: The source authors' own reading of their data, kept separate from the data.
fieldContract.extraction.researchRoleInference: This role's reading, kept separate from both of the above. Inference, not extraction.
fieldContract.extraction.conditionLabels: Index, related or distinct classification per condition, following eligibility plan 2.3. The reasoning for any away-from-index classification is written out.
fieldContract.extraction.contrastType: between-participant, within-participant, or not-applicable, per the frozen U3/EU1 decision.
fieldContract.extraction.translationLadder: Non-null only for non-English sources. Records which rungs of the eligibility plan 4.1 ladder were reached.

separationRule: Three layers are kept apart in every record and must stay apart if these extractions are split into sourceSchema records: what the source reports, what its authors conclude from it, and what this role infers for the project. A claim may cite the first. The second is context. The third is never citable.

question: Q2
extraction.designNote: Single case report, German language.
extraction.translationLadder: Original German. Step 1 (authorised English version): the PubMed record carries an English abstract translation, used for screening. Step 2 (machine-assisted translation): applied on 2026-09-13 to the English abstract and title only, since no full text was obtained. Step 3 (second independent check): not performed. Decision-critical prose from this source therefore cannot support a published claim on its own.

reportedFacts.fact: A 33-year-old patient of normal habitus sustained a humeral rupture of the pectoralis major during recreational sport. He reported sudden onset of left pectoral pain during training on the chest fly machine, together with a whip-like popping sound, followed by immediate painful restriction of movement in the left arm. There was no history of excessive weight training or anabolic steroid use.
reportedFacts.locator: Abstract, Introduction and Case history; read in the original German and through machine translation on 2026-09-13

reportedFacts.fact: The paper states that pectoralis major rupture is a rare injury pattern overall but is frequently described in athletes, particularly in weightlifting, and that the risk is present especially during the eccentric phase of muscle loading. It states that an association with anabolic steroid abuse is described in the literature but that no coherent evidence supports it.

extraction.researchRoleInference: The only retrieved record in which a pectoralis major rupture is attributed to a fly-family exercise. One case, so it establishes that the event can occur on a fly machine and nothing about how often. The translation was machine-assisted and not independently checked, so under the frozen U5/EU4 decision this cannot support a decision-critical prose claim on its own.

question: Q2
extraction.designNote: Within-participant laboratory biomechanics study; four exercises x two loads, order randomised.

conditionLabels.bench press flat: index-X, with grip width standardised and reported
conditionLabels.cable cross-over: related condition (cable fly family). NOT index Y: pulley height is not reported, the elbow angle was not prescribed, and stance is not described, so two or more defining attributes of Y are unreported and eligibility plan section 2.3 rule 3 resolves the classification away from the index set.

reportedFacts.fact: Twenty healthy participants (10 male, 10 female), age 24.9 (SD 2.7) years, height 175.2 (SD 9.0) cm, mass 68.6 (SD 11.1) kg; inclusion 18-45 years with at least two hours per week of weight training experience; exclusion current injury or illness, previous shoulder or upper-limb surgery, neurological disorder or current medical treatment.

Loads were 15 per cent and 30 per cent of body weight for every exercise; six consecutive repetitions per exercise per load, the first discarded, five analysed per side, 200 evaluated cycles in total.
Bench press grip width was standardised as twice upper-arm length plus shoulder width; mean grip width 88.7 (SD 6.7) cm.

Maximum absolute shoulder joint moment, Nm/kg, mean (SD): flat bench press 0.442 (0.046) at 15 per cent BW and 0.760 (0.079) at 30 per cent BW; incline bench press 0.418 (0.041) and 0.712 (0.080); cable cross-over 0.650 (0.113) and 1.026 (0.192); cable pull-over 0.611 (0.086) and 1.09 (0.155).

Maximum absolute shoulder moments were significantly larger for both cable pulley exercises than for both bench press exercises at both loads (p < 0.0125). No significant difference was found between flat and inclined bench press, nor between cable cross-over and cable pull-over.

Elbow flexion-extension range of motion, degrees, mean (SD): flat bench press 79.5 (6.2) at 15 per cent BW and 76.2 (6.4) at 30 per cent BW; cable cross-over 21.8 (10.9) and 32.5 (15.2). Elbow flexion-extension range of motion was significantly larger during the bench press exercises than during the cable pulley exercises.

Elbow flexion-extension maximum joint moment, Nm/kg, mean (SD): flat bench press 0.092 (0.018) and 0.165 (0.041); cable cross-over -0.042 (0.011) and -0.059 (0.017), where positive values correspond to a flexion moment.

Cable pulley exercises showed markedly higher standard deviations in elbow range of motion and moment than the bench press exercises; cable cross-over elbow range of motion increased significantly when load rose from 15 to 30 per cent BW while its elbow maximum moment did not.
Funding: this research received no external funding. Conflicts of interest: the authors declare no conflict of interest. Ethics: ETH Zurich 2017-N-46.

extraction.authorsInterpretation: The authors interpret lower and less fluctuating bench press joint moments as implying more targeted chest-muscle strengthening with less inter-muscular control demand than cable pulley exercises, and recommend combining the two. They also state it is likely that the larger range-of-motion fluctuations during the cross-over led to higher pectoralis activation, and label that as a likelihood inferred from other studies, not as a measurement of their own.
extraction.researchRoleInference: This is the only retrieved study that measures the index press and a cable fly-family condition in the same participants with the same instrumentation. It is mechanical, not adaptive: nothing in it measures muscle size or strength change, so it cannot support any hypertrophy statement. The cable cross-over here is a related condition with an unreported pulley height, so it is not a measurement of index Y.

question: Q2
extraction.designNote: Two-arm randomised trial of volume-equated programmes built entirely from single-joint or entirely from multi-joint exercises.

conditionLabels.multi-joint programme: contains index-X (bench press) among other multi-joint exercises
conditionLabels.single-joint programme: contains related conditions (pec deck machine, incline dumbbell fly, pullover, rear delt fly) among other single-joint exercises

reportedFacts.fact: Thirty-six young male amateur soccer players with no previous resistance-training experience completed 4 weeks of familiarisation and were then randomly assigned to a single-joint group (n = 18; age 23.5 (SD 2.7) years, height 182.1 (SD 5.2) cm) or a multi-joint group (n = 18; age 25.5 (SD 3.8) years, height 185.3 (SD 3.6) cm) for 8 weeks, 3 sessions per week.
reportedFacts.locator: Methods, Study participants and Training program; Results

reportedFacts.fact: Chest work in the multi-joint group was the bench press and incline bench press; chest work in the single-joint group was the pec deck machine and the incline dumbbell fly. Total work volume (repetitions x sets x load) was equated individually during familiarisation; multi-joint sets used 6-8RM, single-joint sets typically 12-18RM, 4 sets per exercise, all sets to momentary failure, all sessions supervised, minimum attendance 80 per cent.

1RM bench press increased 8.1 per cent in the single-joint group and 10.9 per cent in the multi-joint group; the multi-joint increase was significantly greater (p < 0.05, ANCOVA on post values with baseline as covariate). 1RM knee extension increased 12.4 and 18.9 per cent, 1RM squat 8.3 and 13.8 per cent, both favouring multi-joint; VO2max increased 5.1 and 12.5 per cent, favouring multi-joint.
Both groups decreased body fat (6.5 and 11.3 per cent) and increased fat-free mass (3.5 and 4.9 per cent) by DEXA, with no difference between groups. No pectoralis-specific size measure was taken.
Test-retest reliability for 1RM in the authors' laboratory: ICC 0.92 to 0.97.
Conflict of interest: the authors declare the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

extraction.authorsInterpretation: The authors conclude that, at equated total work volume, multi-joint programmes are more efficient than single-joint programmes for muscle strength and maximal oxygen consumption, with no difference in body composition.
extraction.researchRoleInference: This is the closest longitudinal programme-level analogue to the press-versus-fly question that this pass retrieved, and every axis of it is indirect. The contrast is whole programmes rather than two chest exercises; the chest single-joint work is a pec deck and an incline dumbbell fly, not a cable fly; the only upper-body outcome is 1RM bench press, which the multi-joint group practised and the single-joint group did not; and no pectoralis size measure was taken. The task-specificity qualifier is mandatory here.

reportedFacts.fact: Surface EMG was recorded from the sternocostal head of the pectoralis major, the anterior deltoid and the long head of the triceps brachii, normalised to maximal voluntary isometric contraction, during two opposite exercise sequences, each of three sets of 8RM.

For the chest fly, sternocostal pectoralis major activity was 100.13 (SD 13.56) per cent of MVIC in sequence A (chest fly performed second, after the bench press) and 81.47 (SD 13.09) per cent in sequence B.

conditionLabels.upper-half and lower-half bench press: distinct conditions (deliberate partial range of motion)

reportedFacts.fact: Nineteen healthy male volunteers with at least one year of resistance-training experience performed a 10RM bench press across three ranges of motion: full, upper half, and lower half. Sample size was estimated a priori at 17 for f = 0.326, alpha 0.05, power 0.8.

Surface EMG electrodes were placed at four pectoralis major sites: clavicular 15 per cent, sternocostal 15 per cent, clavicular 60 per cent and sternocostal 60 per cent, plus the triceps brachii long and lateral heads and the anterior deltoid.

Mean muscle excitation differed significantly across ranges of motion for all muscles (p < 0.001 to 0.002). Both partial ranges of motion produced greater mean excitation of the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid than the full range of motion.
Peak muscle excitation was significantly greater in the pectoralis major sternocostal 15 per cent region during the upper-half range of motion.

EMG was normalised to the higher of two MVIC positions per muscle; for the pectoralis major these were an isometric bench press with the elbow at about 90 degrees and a supine position with shoulders at 90 degrees flexion and palms pressed together.

question: Q1a
extraction.designNote: Cadaveric imaging and histology of the pectoralis major tendon and its enthesis.

reportedFacts.fact: Fourteen fresh-frozen whole upper-extremity specimens underwent MRI and ultrasound imaging of the pectoralis major muscle, tendon and enthesis, followed by dissection and histology.
The superior-inferior and medial-lateral lengths of the pectoralis major humeral footprint were 75 (SD 9) mm and 7 (SD 1) mm respectively.

The clavicular and sternal head muscles and tendons were identified in all specimens, with the clavicular head tendon generally shorter. Clavicular head tendon medial-lateral length was 19 (SD 8) mm superiorly and 9 (SD 3) mm inferiorly; sternal head tendon 38 (SD 8) mm superiorly and 41 (SD 18) mm inferiorly.

All specimens demonstrated a unilaminar, not bilaminar, enthesis with abundant fibrocartilage on histology. Ultrasound, MRI and histology all failed to identify true tendon layers at the enthesis. Three specimens showed interspersed entheseal fat and loose connective tissue.

The authors state that current descriptions in the literature depict a bilaminar enthesis, which their findings contradict, and suggest that reported delaminating injuries may originate somewhere other than the enthesis.

extraction.authorsInterpretation: The authors conclude that the pectoralis major humeral insertion is a unilaminar fibrocartilaginous enthesis.
extraction.researchRoleInference: This is a direct contradiction of a widely repeated structural description, established with three independent methods in the same specimens. It is carried into the contradiction map and it constrains how the muscle page may describe the insertion.

question: Q1a
extraction.designNote: Cadaveric dissection with Sihler intramuscular nerve staining.

reportedFacts.fact: Forty cadavers of both sexes (22 male, 18 female) gave 80 pectoralis major specimens.

Typical pectoralis major structure was observed in 63.75 per cent of specimens. The most frequent variation was a separate clavicular portion. Hypotrophy of the clavicular portion was seen in one female cadaver (2.5 per cent of specimens); fusion between the clavicular portion and the deltoid was seen in two male cadavers (5 per cent of specimens).

The pectoralis major is mainly innervated by the lateral pectoral nerve. In all specimens stained by the Sihler technique, a contribution of the intercostal nerves to pectoralis major innervation was confirmed.

The paper's introduction describes the typical attachments (clavicular part to the anterior aspect of the medial half of the clavicle; sternocostal part to the anterior sternum and the cartilages of the true ribs; abdominal part to the aponeurosis of the external oblique; insertion at the lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus) and attributes that description to its own reference 1. This is the paper's cited background, not its own observation, and is recorded here as such.

extraction.authorsInterpretation: The authors argue that pectoralis major variations affect pectoral nerve innervation patterns and matter surgically.
extraction.researchRoleInference: Two usable facts: roughly a third of specimens departed from the textbook configuration, which bounds how categorically the muscle page may describe structure; and intercostal nerve contribution was present in every stained specimen, which complicates the simple lateral-nerve-to-clavicular-head, medial-nerve-to-sternocostal-head account found in tertiary references.
